INTERVENORS SUZANNE C. JAMES’ AND BRUCE L. JAMES’, INDIVIDUALLY AND AS REPRESENTATIVES OF REATA RIVER RANCH, LP’S 	INITIAL BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (ALJ) AND COMMISSIONERS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION: 

COME NOW, Suzanne C. James (S. James) and Bruce L. James (B. James), Individually (collectively the Jameses) and as Representatives of the Reata River Ranch, LP, (the Reata), Intervenors in the above entitled and numbered matter before the Public Utility Commission, and, after the close of evidence of the hearing on the merits, file this their Initial Brief in response to Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (Oncor) and LCRA TSC’s (LCRA) (collectively Applicants) Application to Amend their Application for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a Proposed 765-kV Transmission Line from their Bell County East Switch to their Big Hill Substation.  In support of this Initial Brief, Intervenors S. James, B. James, and the Reata would respectfully show that the ALJs and PUC Commission should deny the Application due to procedural irregularities, prejudicial admission of evidence favoring the utilities, the denial of these Intervenors right to cross-examination, and inadequate data analysis or alternatively, deny any route within the San Saba River Basin in McCulloch, Mason and Menard Counties, in particular Links K63, L2, M23, M22, L1, M32, M33, and M8, and would argue the following:
Introduction
1.	Intervenors S. James, B. James, and the Reata live and ranch in the rural county of McCulloch (See Exhibit 1, S. James’ Admitted Direct Testimony, Reata 000005-6) and believe the admitted record shows many deficiencies in the Joint Application of Oncor and the LCRA (See J. Luther King, Admitted Direct and Rebuttal Testimony, Items Nos. 4440 and 5026 and also Expert Testimony of James E. Scott, III, Item Nos. 4507 and 5086).  Even many of Applicants own witnesses including their Environmental Assessment (EA), as did most of the Intervenors witnesses, identifies significant impacts to the Hill Country environment that were not included by Applicants that include, wildlife (deer, turkey, exotics), agriculture and ranching operations, livestock (cattle, goats and sheep), residences and special use buildings, sensitive uses, water resources (rivers, streams, creeks, ponds, wells, water troughs), flooding, cultural and historical resources, and community values. Most of Applicants’ witnesses admitted that their review of all Route Links was mainly done via desktop aerial maps and geophysical maps, or what they could see from main highways.  The location of Link M22 is more than 4.5 miles from Reata’s front gate and cannot be seen from State Highway 190. Incredibly, the lack of serious study of the impact of the San Saba River and its tributaries, all being located in the “Flash Flood Alley” of Central Texas is difficult to overlook by any reasonably prudent transmission line operator. Joint Applicants have totally ignored the devastation that occurred with the record flood of July 2025 which impact a year later is still being felt by ranchers along the San Saba River and how they would prepare for a recurrence of the same.  For this deficiency alone, the Joint Application should be denied.
II.	Overview of Evidentiary and Procedural Issues
2.	Intervenors S. James, B. James, and the Reata due to Intervenor B. James being an attorney at law (See Exhibit 2, Bruce L. James’ Admitted Direct Testimony, Reata 000021), note at least three major issues that cast a shadow of unfairness over this proceeding that would suggest a procedural bias for the utilities in light of ALJ rulings in the hearing on the merits.  
3.	First, Motions to Conduct a Route Adequacy Hearing were filed in this matter by:  (1) 4K Land and Cattle Company’s (4K) Statement Challenging Route Adequacy and their Request for a Hearing on the same (Item No. 3686) ; (2) Burnet County Commissioner’s Court (Burnet) Route Adequacy Challenge and Request for Hearing (Item No. 3679); and (3) Save the Lampasas’ (Lampasas) Route Adequacy Challenge (Item No. 3686).  Several Intervenors also announced their support for these three route adequacy challenges.  No hearing was held on these motions by the ALJ as is supposedly provided for by SOAH Order No. 6.  Instead, the ALJs summarily ruled with no need for an adequacy hearing.  This ruling has been appealed to the Commission which has placed the item on an upcoming meeting of the whole. 
4.	Second, is the clouded admission of Applicants’ Exhibit No. 33, entitled “Memo” dated June 10, 2026 (Emphasis added) to Governor Greg Abbott and others from the Texas Oil & Gas Association, Permian Basin Petroleum Association, Texas Alliance of Energy Producers, Texas Independent Producers & Royalty Owners Association, and the Texas Pipeline Association, none of whom were parties to this proceeding.  Applicant LCRA’s counsel cleverly asked the Staff’s expert witness John Poole, P.E., on that very day June 10, 2026, if he had seen the “Memo” without showing it on a screen or allowing any time for all other intervening parties to have the opportunity to review in detail, reflect upon, and formulate any objections to Applicants’ Exhibit 33. (See Transcript for Hearing on the Merits, June 10, 2026, pp. 236, ll. 22-25; 237, ll. 1-25; 238, ll. 1-3; 242, ll. 18-25; 243, ll. 1-7). Exhibit 33 was not sponsored by its author (who was never identified) or by any recipient to whom the Memo was addressed.  Exhibit 33 was not properly authenticated, was never produced by Applicants in discovery, was not listed as an Exhibit in pre-hearing filings, and only appeared on the morning of June 10 in the middle of the hearing on the merits.  Exhibit 33 is a blatant hearsay document adding Direct Testimony by Applicants from an unknown author whose knowledge of the facts asserted in the “Memo” cannot be tested by cross-examination, especially in light of what happened at the end of the hearing on the merits addressed next.  It unfairly prohibits Intervenors from designating the author of the Memo for cross-examination on their own witness lists.  Exhibit 33 should be stricken from the record for unfair trial tactics by Applicants’ counsel and lack of evidentiary basis.
5.	Third, is the baffling refusal to allow fellow McCulloch County Intervenors Bruce James and Gerald Nobles to cross-exam each other that they had properly designated on their cross-examination witness list.  Few rights in the trial of contested matters are more sacred than the right to cross-exam other witnesses whether they are friendly or not.  Intervenors already had imposed upon their right to cross-examination a three (3) minute time limit by the ALJs.  The  daily time for the hearing to be over was 5:00 PM.  The denial of these Intervenors, the last two witnesses to be called in this matter, to cross-examine each other when viewed with the ALJs allowance of new evidence to be submitted by Applicants (Exhibit 33) again suggests a procedural bias for the utilities considering  previous ALJs’ rulings.  So why is the right to cross-exam any witness of an Intervenors choosing so important?
III.	The PUC Procedural Right to Cross-Examination
6.	Reata’s and L Bar’s Motion to Reconsider and Offer of Proof (Item No. 6138) at the time of this writing has not been ruled upon by the ALJs. 
7.	The purpose of a system of procedures is to “promote the just and efficient disposition of proceedings and public participation in the decision-making process.”  PUC Proc. R. §22.1(a). (Emphasis added).  The ALJs refusal to allow Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles (members of the public and Intervenors) to conduct cross examination of each other denied them “public participation in the decision making process.”  
8.	The PUC specifically declares that the Texas Rules of Evidence “…must be followed in contested cases.” PUC Proc. R. §22.221(a). (Emphasis added).  As stated in the Texas Rules of Evidence, in the Purpose section:  “These rules should be construed so as to administer every proceeding fairly, eliminate unjustifiable expense and delay, and promote the development of evidence law, to the end of ascertaining the truth and securing a just determination.”  Tex. R. Evid. 102. (Emphasis added).  
9.	Applicants’ (and others) objection to Intervenors B. James’ and G. Nobles’ cross-examination testimony attempted to be offered as the last two witnesses in the weeklong hearing of this matter was “they are aligned,” “James & Nobles being members of The San Saba River Alliance," it is “friendly cross-examination,” and their testimony (though never heard) “is merely supplementing their previously filed direct testimony.”  The ALJ’s sustained Applicants’ objections and Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles were denied the fundamental right to testify though duly designated for cross-examination under SOAH’s Orders in this matter.  (See Transcript of Hearing on the Merits, June 12, 2026, pp. 209, ll. 2-19; 223, ll. 1-18; 226, ll. 11-25; 227, ll. 1-25; 228, ll. 1-25; 229, ll. 1-25; 230, ll.  1-16; Item 6138, Exhibits 1 and 2).  
10.	As noted by the authors of  the Treatise, McCormick on Evidence:  “For two centuries, common law judges and lawyers have regarded the opportunity for cross-examination as an essential safeguard of the accuracy and completeness of testimony.  They have insisted that the opportunity is a right, not a mere privilege.  This right is available at the taking of depositions as well as during the examination of witnesses at trial.”  See McCormick on Evidence §19 ( 8th Ed. 2020); Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(c).  When considering the traditional rule of wide-open cross-examination, the same authors explain that:  “ …the cross-examiner is not limited to the topics which the direct examiner has chosen to open.  The cross-examiner is free to question about any subject relevant to any issue on the merits of the entire case, including facts relating solely to cross-examiner’s own case or affirmative defenses.”  See McCormick on Evidence §21 ( 8th Ed. 2020).  (Emphasis added). The ALJs had already decided to time-limit (only 3 minutes) the Intervenors’ right to cross-examination but to deny that right altogether is simply a step too far in light of the mandate found in PUC Proc. R. §22.221(a) that the Texas Rules of Evidence must be followed in contested cases.
IV.	The Alignment Objection by Applicants 
11.	With regard to alignment, PUC Proc. R. §22.105 reads:
“Parties, except for the Office of Public Utility Counsel and the commission staff representing the public interest, may be aligned for the purposes of participating in a hearing or portions of a hearing if the parties have the same positions on issues of fact or law. To the extent alignment is determined to be necessary, the presiding officer shall order alignment of the parties at the earliest reasonable opportunity so as to avoid unnecessary duplication of effort and to allow aligned parties an adequate opportunity to prepare for hearing. The presiding officer may limit the number of representatives of aligned parties who conduct cross-examination of any particular witness during the hearing on the merits.”

12.	There was never a motion by Applicants to determine the necessity of alignment, let alone an Order by the ALJs ordering alignment of Intervenors the Jameses and their ranch Reata  and the Nobles and L Bar’s River and Voca Ranches.    Intervenors had timely designated their witnesses for cross-examination and were never sought to be aligned until Friday, June 12, 2026, around 3:00 PM at the close of the hearing.  A simple reading of the Intervenors Direct Testimony and attached Offers of Proof to their Motion to Reconsider Iitem 6138) show that they are not completely aligned.  Here are some of the major factual differences:
(1)	The Jameses Reata ranch is located in Precinct 1 of McCulloch County while the L Bar River and Voca Ranches are located in Precinct 2.
(2)	The Jameses gain access to the Reata ranch off of State Highway 190 west (the Menard Highway) and the Nobles gain access to the L Bar River ranch off of US Highway 87 and the Voca Ranch off of US Highway 71. The drive to each other’s ranch is approximately 25 miles. 
(3)	The James’ and Reata’s Motion to Intervene show that their concern is with Route Links M22, M11 and M12 (Item 378, Page 2) while the Nobles’ and L Bar’s Motion to Intervene show their concern is with Route Links M22 (River Ranch) and K51(Voca Ranch) (Item 829, Page 2). 
(4)	Neither Intervenor B. James nor Intervenor G. Nobles belong to an entity named the San Saba River Alliance.  Applicants’ counsel obviously misspoke on that issue and gave a false reason to claim James and Nobles were to be considered aligned. The San Saba River Alliance, if such exists, is not a party to this proceeding and if that was a concern to Applicants, such should have been raised in a Motion to Align.  Having failed to do so, such argument should be considered waived.
13.	It appears from a review of the issue of alignment that alignment is optional and should only occur if parties share the same positions on issues of fact or law.  Here no Order of Alignment ever occurred, only an objection that the parties are aligned.  Alignment does not in and of itself remove the right to cross-examine — it only allows the presiding officer to limit the number of aligned representatives who may question a single witness.  Intervenors are treated as full parties in PUC proceedings and have the same procedural rights as other parties, including the right to present evidence, file motions, and participate in discovery and cross-examination.  Even if an intervenor is aligned with another party, they are not prohibited from asking cross-examination questions. The only potential restriction is that the presiding officer may limit the number of aligned representatives who can question a given witness to avoid duplication and ensure fair preparation.  It is hard to imagine that the remaining two witnesses in the hearing on the merits who were only allotted three (3) minutes each with over two hours until the 5:00 PM wrap up time would have unduly delayed this matter in any way.
14.	The exclusion of Intervenors B. James’ and G. Nobles’ Cross-Examination testimony on June 12, 2026 around 3:00 PM on the last day of the hearing in light of the circumstances explained below, is unjust, prevents Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles complete participation in the proceeding as members of the public, is unfair in light of the disproportionate resources available to Applicants’ legal squads and the ALJ’s rulings on late filed testimony of Applicants (Exhibit 33) and other parties as well as so-called “friendly” cross-examination of previous witnesses, would not have caused an unjustifiable delay since their testimony was limited by Order of the ALJ’s to no more than three (3) minutes, and will help secure a just determination in this matter.
V.	Due Process and Cross-Examination Limitations

	15.	Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles have never been a party to, or participated in, or testified in a PUC hearing until this matter, which must be described as an expedited, compressed proceeding at best.  Intervenors S. James, B. James, and the Reata timely designated Intervenor G. Nobles as a witness who had filed his Direct Testimony in this matter as a witness they would like to cross-examine in this matter.  Likewise, Intervenors D. Nobles, G. Nobles, and the L Bar timely designated Intervenor B. James as a witness who had filed his Direct Testimony in this matter as a witness they would like to cross-examine in this matter. 
16.	Applicants and certain other parties apparently were opposed to the Jameses and the Nobles’ views, sought to limit cross-examination to only what was presented via written Direct Testimony or written Rebuttal Testimony in this matter.  The ALJ’s seem to have agreed although at times allowing other parties to pursue what was by the ALJs and some parties euphemistically called “friendly cross.”
17.	When the PUC specifically declared that the Texas Rules of Evidence “…must be followed in contested cases,” (PUC Proc. R. §22.221(a)), it did not exclude Tex. R. Evid. 611(b) . (Emphasis added).  Tex. R. Evid. 611(b) reads: “Scope of Cross-Examination.  A witness may be cross-examined on any relevant matter, including credibility.” (Emphasis added.)  Nowhere in the PUC Procedural Rules is there an attempt to exclude the breadth and scope of Tex. R. Evid. 611(b).
18.	As Intervenor B. James argued, Tex. R. Evid. 611(b) allows wide open cross-examination of witnesses, following traditional Texas practice. Wentworth v. Crawford, 11 Tex. 127, 133 (1853).  “While trial courts have wide discretion in controlling the form and manner of cross-examination, their discretion is considerably more limited when it comes to the scope of cross-examination…” . Brown & Rondon, Texas Rules of Evidence Handbook, p. 648 (2025). (Emphasis added).   “Cross-examination is frequently extolled as the single best mechanism for discovering the truth; any limitations on its legitimate scope are strictly reviewed.” Brown & Rondon, Texas Rules of Evidence Handbook, p. 648 (2025).  Cross-examination is a safeguard essential to a fair trial and a cornerstone in the quest for truth.  Davidson v. Great Nat’l Life Ins., 737 S.W.2d 312, 314 (Tex. 1987).  
19.	Intervenor B. James also argued that denial of Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles’ right to cross-exam is a denial of procedural due process,  In this proceeding to establish a preferred route for a never before tried 765 kV transmission line, the ultimate effect is to take many of the Intervenors private property (land) away from them. The Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution protects against deprivation of life, liberty, or property, by the State “without due process of law.”  U.S. Const. amend. XIV; Daniels v. Williams, 474 U.S. 327, 331, 106 S.Ct. 662 (1986). 
20.	The Texas Constitution provides that “No citizen of this State shall be deprived of life, liberty, property, privileges or immunities, or in any manner disenfranchised, except by the due course of the law of the land.”  Tex. Const. art. I, §19.  The Texas “due course” and federal “due process” have been interpreted to be without meaningful distinction.”  Univ. of Tex. Med. School at Houston v. Than, 901 S.W. 2d 926, 929 (Tex. 1995). 
21.	Although implicating the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment in criminal matters (applied to the States through the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment), where the government seeks to take away an individual’s liberty rights, the United States Supreme Court has said:  “Denial of cross-examination …would be constitutional error of the first magnitude and no amount of showing of want of prejudice would cure it.”  Brookhart v. Janis, 384 U.S. 1, 3, 86 S. Ct. 1245  (1966). 
22.	Importantly, as shown in Exhibits 1 (Intervenor B. James’ Offer of Proof) and Exhibit 2 (Intervenor G. Nobles Offer of Proof)(Item 6138), their testimony addresses in part testimony allowed into evidence at the hearing on the merits never heard or offered before in evidence.  In the direct testimony of Applicants’ witness Jared Gurley, he offered evidence that in the last ten (10) years in the Permian Basin no new power generating facilities had been constructed as though that in and of itself was justification for Applicants’ CCN.  The most egregious new evidence was offered by the Applicants, Exhibit 33.  It was admitted.  It was the June 10, 2026 “Memo” to the Governor, et al, from the Texas Oil & Gas Association, et al (none whom were parties to this matter) offered by Applicants that was not properly authenticated, not part of Applicants’ Direct or Rebuttal Testimony (how could it be since it did not exist until June 10 in the middle of the hearing on the merits), was not sponsored by its author (which was not the Applicants or any party to this docket), and contained factual assertions offered as new direct testimony from other sources not in evidence.  The Memo of June 10, 2026, is some unidentified person or persons direct testimony that should be stricken from the record in the first instance but if not stricken, then Intervenors B. James and G. Nobles were not allowed to dispute or respond by way of cross-examination to such new evidence that first appeared two days before.
23.	The unfairness of the above sequence of events demands a new trial on the merits and recognition that the PUC rules as to following the Texas Rules of Evidence are imperative, not at the whim of the utilities.  
VI.	Needs and Route Arguments Summary
	24.	As the PUC and ALJs v certainly understand and as clearly gleaned from the totality of the hearing on the merits, transmission lines do not generate electricity. The proposed first of its kind in Texas 765-kV facilities running through Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties would transport power, but it would not add generation capacity to the ERCOT system or create new supply for the Permian Basin. Nor would this new line provide the citizens of any of these counties with electricity, only a memory of what their land used to look like.  So, Applicants’ Joint Application simply won't solve the problem of providing Texans with more reliable or less expensive energy.  It simply moves what is believed to be excess energy from the Bell County area in the Interstate I-35 corridor, also a fast-growing population area that will need electricity too and more generating facilities in the future.
A.	Needs
25.	With regard to the needs issue, as reviewed and covered at the hearing by numerous witnesses, House Bill 5066 required ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin. It does not appear to predetermine the outcome of that planning process, nor did it require ERCOT to assume that reliability must be achieved through only long-distance imports from outside the region. The statute directs ERCOT to develop a plan that addresses reliability concerns. Nothing in House Bill 5066 prohibited ERCOT from studying whether local generation resources could satisfy some or all of those same reliability objectives in addition to or excluding the building of import transmission lines.
26.	What the utilities refer to as the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (Plan) in  large part assumed only a future in which substantial generation remains located outside the Permian Basin and electricity reliability is maintained through long-distance imports into the region. With the Permian Basin’s high natural gas resources and a natural gas generating power plant being the most efficient means of electricity generation, why not build on location in the Permian Basin? In the Plan, ERCOT then evaluated the transmission facilities necessary to support that assumed generation geography. What ERCOT did not do was evaluate whether different, plausible generation-development scenarios-including greater local generation development in or near the Permian Basin-would materially alter the transmission solution required to achieve the same reliability objectives.  As suggested in Intervenors testimony, who is really pushing this approach?  Is it really the oil and gas companies or is it new data center projects that need both large amounts of electricity and water? 
27.	As best can be seen, ERCOT never evaluated whether its recommendation for approximately 1,255 miles of new 765-kV transmission infrastructure was dependent upon assumptions concerning where future power generation would be located. Studying alternative scenarios to supply future needs of electricity to the Permian Basin (or anywhere) would have been a prudent way to plan.  None of Applicants’ filings showed any effort in such planning because it’s not to their financial benefit.  Evaluating whether increased local power generation plants would clearly reduce the need for this massive transmission line expansion should have occurred.  Applicants failed to identify any study in which ERCOT, or any other utility, oil and gas concern, or data center analyzed whether increased local generation development could reduce the need for the 765-kV import paths across the Hill Country of Texas. Nor do Applicants refute testimony acknowledging that such alternatives were not studied. Instead, Applicants simply assumed ipse dixit that transmission was the correct answer because transmission is the mechanism selected by ERCOT.  And besides that, it is their business,
28.	 The three or four projects now before the PUC for and approximately 1,255 miles of new, extra-high voltage 765-kV infrastructure at issue represent nearly $33 billion in transmission investment. Once approved and constructed, those investments by the utilities will be billed back to Texas ratepayers for decades. Such a deal.  The public interest and the interest of the State of Texas is not served by rushing through approval of these transmission line facilities on an expedited basis whose necessity remains subject to legitimate dispute and public debate. As one interested party put it: “The Commission's obligation is to make the correct decision based on a complete understanding of the facts and in the best interests of Texas consumers, not merely the fastest decision based on Applicants' preferred schedule.”
B.	Routing
29.	With regard to routing, which is the Applicants’ unique way to deflect from their Applications shortcomings and to pit neighbor against neighbor.  As the ALJs should recall and the Commission should read in the transcript, most of the Intervenors were against all Routes, especially the Intervenors in McCulloch County including the McCulloch County Commissioners Court.  What was of the most concern to Intervenors in general was: (1) the accuracy of the number of habitable structures on each route including Applicants’ failure at totally missing a new elementary school, (2) the accuracy of any route that is parallel to property boundaries because this data is based on parcel boundaries and not owner property boundaries, and (3) the failure to properly notice affected landowners when new Links were added after the initial public meetings.  These deficiencies should also be cause for denial of the Joint Application.
30.	It became glaringly apparent during the hearing on the merits, that Applicants Oncor and LCRA used routing software with completely outdated geographic data, unverified subdivision maps, unverified property ownership, or sweeping regional generalizations, so they could create a perfect-on-paper route that the utilities would utilize. When questioned about problems that could arise, how many times was the response that the utilities would work it out with the landowner.  Many of the utilities’ witnesses were forced to admit they completely failed to account for active real estate developments, local hunting businesses, certain school structures, and critical ecological features on the ground that they simply overlooked or thought no one would bring up. Oncor's and LCRA’s claimed "perfect compliance" narrative was nothing more than an uncoordinated, speculative mess that requires denial of their Joint Application in toto.
31.	With regard to the Reata, it is a pristine multi-generational family ranch started in 1897 and Applicants’ proposed Link M22 would fractionalize our ranch almost dividing it in the middle as it would to our deceased cousin’s ranch the Q- Ranch and our nieces ranch, the Gray TV Ranch. which all belonged to our family’s patriarch T. Gray.  (See S. James Admitted Direct Testimony, Exhibit 1, Reata 000006, 000009, 000010; B. James Admitted Direct Testimony, Exhibit 2, Reata 000022, 000025, 000026).  There is no evidence presented by Applicants why this Link so close to the San Saba River was selected.  There is no evidence (1) that Reata ranch has an existing right of way through it, (2) that Reata ranch has ever been “disturbed,” (3) that Reata ranch lacks environmental integrity, or (4) that the McCulloch County community values favor bisecting large ranches.  (See Transcript of June 11, 2026, Testimony of former Commissioner Barry T. Smitherman, pp. 168, ll. 16-25; 169, ll. 1-4, 13-25; 170, ll. 1-25; 171, ll. 1-7; 189, ll. 13-24).  The Reata is a multi-generational ranch with no existing transmission lines running through its boundaries, has never been disturbed from its front gate to the south side of the San Saba River, is environmentally sound and undisturbed and its community values clearly are against bisecting the ranch.  M22 ignores these requirements and thus does not follow PURA provisions and rules and is therefore a link right of way not in compliance with statutes or rules of the PUC. (See Transcript of June 11, 2026, Testimony of former Commissioner Barry T. Smitherman, pp. 170, ll. 20-25; 171, ll. 1-7).  Further, the San Saba River is designated as an ecologically significant stream segment and an impaired waterway under Section 303(d) of the Clean Water Act.
C.	The CCG Created Route
32.	One of the suggested routes for the ALJs and PUC to consider was created by witness Rae Lynn Schneider Reinchke on behalf of three (3) Intervenors Segment K13/K51 Landowners, Cherokee Creek Partners, and Bonnie Helene McAnelly, Individually and as Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and Bonnie Helene McAnelly 2023 Trust.  (See Direct Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider,  Item 4204; Rebuttal Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke, Item 5048; Transcript of Hearing on the Merits, June 11, 2026, pp. 218-251).  This route includes the use of M22 running parallel to the San Saba River and is within the San Saba River basin.
33.	Ms. Reinchke’s suggested route was heavily criticized by Will McAdams in his Cross-Rebuttal Testimony.  (See Cross Rebuttal Testimony of Will McAdams, Item No. 5052).  As gleaned from the cross-examination record of Ms. Reinchke noted above and the testimony of Mr. McAdams, the problems with Route CCG are numerous and include:
(1)	Route CCG was not one of the 122 Routes suggested by Applicants nor was Route CCG in Oncor/LCRA’s “Top 6” strongest performing routes for the transmission project.
